def-parametric-survival-and-reliability:
## Definition

Let $T$ be a nonnegative event time as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]],
with law $P_T$. Its cumulative distribution function is
$F_T(t)=P(T\le t)$ ([[def-cumulative-distribution-function-of-a-random-variable]]).
The **survival function** is
$$S_T(t):=P(T>t)=1-F_T(t),\qquad t\ge0.$$
Write $S_T(t^-):=P(T\ge t)$ for the pre-event survival. In particular,
$S_T(0)=1$ exactly when $P(T=0)=0$.

For a **nonrepairable** unit, meaning that a failed unit is permanently removed
from the population, its **reliability function** is
$R_T(t):=P(T>t)=S_T(t)$. This is a single first-failure lifetime model. A
repairable system can fail repeatedly; its cumulative failure count and rate of
occurrence of failures are not summarized by this one-lifetime survival
function.

When the law of $T$ has a specified density $f$ relative to Lebesgue measure,
meaning $P_T(A)=\int_A f(u)\,du$ for each Borel set $A$, and $S_T(t)>0$, its
**density hazard** is the chosen-version function
$$\lambda_T(t):=\frac{f(t)}{S_T(t)}.$$
Values can change on a Lebesgue-null set when the density representative
changes. Where this hazard is integrable, the **cumulative hazard** is
$$\Lambda_T(t):=\int_0^t\lambda_T(u)\,du.$$
For a law that may have an atom at $t$, its **jump hazard** is
$$q_T(t):=\frac{P(T=t)}{P(T\ge t)}$$
when $P(T\ge t)>0$. The jump hazard is a conditional event probability, rather
than a density per unit time.

For parameters $\lambda>0$, the **exponential survival specification** is
$S_T(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$; the family of laws is denoted
$T\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$. For shape $k>0$ and scale $\eta>0$, the
**Weibull survival specification** is
$S_T(t)=e^{-(t/\eta)^k}$ for $t\ge0$. These are parameter-indexed families of
sampling laws in the sense of [[def-parametric-statistical-model]]; their
existence and densities are established in
[[thm-exponential-and-weibull-survival-laws]].

The density-hazard identity for absolutely continuous event-time laws and the
jump relation for atoms are separate results. An empirical pattern such as a
decreasing-then-increasing “bathtub” hazard is not a consequence of these
definitions or of either parametric family.
thm-exponential-and-weibull-survival-law:
## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. For $\lambda>0$, the density
$$f_\lambda(t)=\begin{cases}\lambda e^{-\lambda t},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law on $\mathbb R$ with survival
$S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$. For $k,\eta>0$, the density
$$f_{k,\eta}(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}e^{-(t/\eta)^k},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law with survival $S(t)=e^{-(t/\eta)^k}$ for $t\ge0$.
Each law is unique among probability laws on $[0,\infty)$ with that survival.
The density hazards are respectively $\lambda$ and
$\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}$ for $t>0$.
thm-survival-cumulative-hazard-identity:
## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $T$ be a nonnegative event
time with a finite-valued density $f$ relative to Lebesgue measure, so
$P_T(A)=\int_A f(u)\,du$ for every Borel $A\subseteq[0,\infty)$, and assume
$S_T(0)=1$. Let
$$\tau_*:=\inf\{t\ge0:S_T(t)=0\},$$
with $\tau_*=+\infty$ if this set is empty. For every $0\le t<\tau_*$,
$$S_T(t)=\exp\!\left(-\int_0^t\frac{f(u)}{S_T(u)}\,du\right).$$
If $\tau_*<\infty$, the improper cumulative hazard tends to $+\infty$ as
$t\uparrow\tau_*$; extending it by $+\infty$ for $t\ge\tau_*$ gives the same
identity there with the convention $e^{-\infty}=0$. The density-hazard formula
is asserted only where $S_T>0$.
thm-jump-hazard-survival-product:
## Statement

Assume Countable Choice. Let $T\ge0$ have CDF $F_T(t)=P(T\le t)$ and
survival $S_T(t)=P(T>t)$. For any $t\ge0$ with $S_T(t^-)=P(T\ge t)>0$, define
the atomic hazard
$$q_T(t):=\frac{P(T=t)}{P(T\ge t)}.$$
Then
$$S_T(t)=S_T(t^-)(1-q_T(t)).$$

In particular, if $m\ge1$ and the law is supported on a finite set of distinct times
$0\le t_1<\cdots<t_m$ and each listed point has positive mass, put
$q_j:=q_T(t_j)$. Then
$$S_T(t_j)=\prod_{r=1}^{j}(1-q_r),\qquad 1\le j\le m.$$
For laws with both continuous and atomic parts, the pointwise jump identity
still holds at every atom; this finite-support product is not a formula for the
continuous decrease between atoms.
thm-censored-exponential-likelihood-and-:
## Statement

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $\lambda>0$ be an event-rate parameter and let $\psi\in\Psi$ index a
censoring-law family $G_\psi$ on $[0,\infty)$. For every $\psi$, assume
$G_\psi$ has a specified finite-valued density $g_\psi$ relative to one fixed
sigma-finite measure $\nu$, where $\nu$ does not depend on $\lambda$ or $\psi$.
Assume the parameter space is the product $(0,\infty)\times\Psi$: the event
law depends only on $\lambda$, the censor law only on $\psi$, and for each
subject $T_i\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ is independent of $C_i\sim G_\psi$.
The subject pairs are iid. Observe
$$U_i=\min(T_i,C_i),\qquad \delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\},$$
as in [[def-event-time-observation-schemes]]. Write
$\bar G_\psi(u):=G_\psi([u,\infty))$.

On the one-subject observation space $[0,\infty)\times\{0,1\}$, let $\rho$
equal Lebesgue measure on the $\delta=1$ branch and $\nu$ on the $\delta=0$
branch; explicitly,
$$\rho(A)=\operatorname{Leb}\{u:(u,1)\in A\}+\nu\{u:(u,0)\in A\}$$
for measurable $A$. Then the observation law has the explicitly specified $\rho$-density
$$h_{\lambda,\psi}(u,1)=\lambda e^{-\lambda u}\bar G_\psi(u),\qquad h_{\lambda,\psi}(u,0)=e^{-\lambda u}g_\psi(u).$$
For $n\ge1$ subjects, set $d:=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_i$ and
$E:=\sum_{i=1}^n U_i$. For each fixed $(\lambda,\psi)$ and its displayed
density versions, the likelihood is, $\rho^{\otimes n}$-almost everywhere,
$$L(\lambda,\psi;\mathbf u,\boldsymbol\delta)=\lambda^d e^{-\lambda E}C_\psi(\mathbf u,\boldsymbol\delta),$$
where
$$C_\psi(\mathbf u,\boldsymbol\delta):=\prod_{i:\delta_i=1}\bar G_\psi(u_i)\prod_{i:\delta_i=0}g_\psi(u_i).$$
Thus, for fixed $\psi$ with $C_\psi>0$, the event-rate likelihood is
proportional to $\lambda^d e^{-\lambda E}$.

For such data: if $d>0$ and $E>0$, the unique maximum over $\lambda>0$ is
$\widehat\lambda=d/E$; if $d=0$ and $E>0$, the likelihood is strictly
decreasing, with supremum as $\lambda\downarrow0$ and no maximizer in
$(0,\infty)$. A formal likelihood extension to the boundary $\lambda=0$
attains that supremum there, but $\lambda=0$ is not a proper exponential law
for finite event times. If $d=0$ and $E=0$, the likelihood is constant in
$\lambda$. Under the model, $d>0,E=0$ occurs with probability zero. If
$C_\psi=0$, the likelihood version is zero for every $\lambda$ at that fixed
$\psi$, so the stated maximizing claims do not apply to that parameter value.
